newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China project funding opportune for HK banks - Chase.
newsitem.headline: China project funding opportune for HK banks - Chase.

text.p: China's funding requirements of an estimated US$1 trillion for infrastructure investment over the next decade offers immense opportunities to Hong Kong banks but not without risk, a leading banker said on Wednesday.

Traditionally, around 10 to 20 percent of China's infrastructure investment will be financed through offshore sources, Antony Leung, Chase Manhattan Bank's managing director and regional manager for Greater China and the Philippines, told a symposium.
Leung said it was estimated China would need more than US$1 trillion over the next decade to upgrade its infrastructure.
Hong Kong, the as yet unchallenged financial centre for China, is expected to continue its key role as a major source of capital for mainland projects, he said.
But Leung said there was concern over the risk associated with non-recourse financing for Chinese infrastructure projects.

Beijing's decision in 1993 to limit guarantees provided by Chinese financial institutions has reduced the syndicated loan market as a major source of financing for infrastructure projects, Leung said.
With banks no longer able to rely on blanket guarantees from Chinese financial institutions, they must provide loans on a project basis, Leung said.
"It is difficult to arrange project finance on a non-recourse basis," Leung said, adding that China's legal system was to blame.
He also urged wider acceptance among Chinese authorities of a true build-operate-transfer (BOT) strucuture, which would be "extremely helpful" for project financing.
Some borrowers are compelled to branch out their sources of funds, such as the U.S. 144a market, he said.

Zhuhai Highway Co took the lead in tapping the international bond market with its the first true non-recourse infrastructure 144a bond transaction, which was offered to U.S. investors by lead manager Morgan Stanley in August.
Leung said the successful deal became the model for upcoming infrastructure projects in China, adding that he expected more borrowers to follow suit.
Looking ahead, he said there would be more issues involving Chinese projects next year than in 1996, with aircraft financing deals expected.
